lesson.title: The Nervous System's Support Crew
lesson.summary: Glial cells are the non-neuronal cells that insulate axons, supply nutrients, clean up debris, and defend the nervous system, and without them neurons could not transmit signals efficiently or survive.
lesson.body:
Neurons could not do their job alone. Surrounding and supporting them are the glial cells, sometimes called neuroglia, a name that comes from the Greek word for glue. Glial cells actually outnumber neurons in much of the nervous system, and while they do not typically fire the kind of long-distance electrical signals that define neurons, they are essential for keeping neurons alive, properly insulated, and able to communicate efficiently.

One major job of glial cells is producing the myelin sheath introduced earlier as part of neuron structure. In the central nervous system, cells called oligodendrocytes wrap segments of myelin around multiple nearby axons. In the peripheral nervous system, a different cell type called Schwann cells performs the same job, but each Schwann cell wraps myelin around just one axon. This division of labor matters because damage in the central and peripheral nervous systems can affect myelin differently, and it explains why some nerve conditions are limited to the brain and spinal cord while others affect nerves throughout the body.

Astrocytes, another major glial type, perform a broader support role. They help form the blood-brain barrier that controls which substances can pass from the bloodstream into brain tissue, supply neurons with nutrients, and clean up excess neurotransmitters from the synapse after a signal has been sent, which helps keep neural communication precise rather than smeared out over time. Astrocytes also provide structural scaffolding that helps guide the growth of axons during development and supports repair processes after injury.

A third type, microglia, act as the nervous system's resident immune cells. They patrol brain and spinal cord tissue, clearing away dead cells, debris, and pathogens, and become especially active after injury or infection. A fourth type, ependymal cells, line the fluid filled ventricles of the brain and help produce and circulate cerebrospinal fluid, the fluid that cushions the brain and spinal cord and helps clear away metabolic waste. Without this cleanup crew, damaged tissue in the brain would have no way to be repaired or cleared.

The importance of glial cells becomes obvious when they stop working properly. In multiple sclerosis, the immune system mistakenly attacks and damages myelin in the central nervous system, disrupting the oligodendrocytes that maintain it. As myelin breaks down, the axons underneath lose their insulation, and electrical signals that once traveled quickly and efficiently begin to slow, weaken, or fail to reach their destination at all, producing symptoms like muscle weakness, numbness, and coordination problems that depend on which myelinated pathways are affected. The disease is a vivid illustration of how much healthy neural function depends on the quiet, supportive work glial cells do behind the scenes.
